items.explanation: Synnduit uses MEF: [Feed]/[Sink] mark discoverable parts the engine finds automatically — there's no Startup/Program registration call.

misconceptions.a: That's Microsoft.Extensions.DI; Synnduit composes with MEF attributes instead.

items.stem: What do `[Export(typeof(ICourseService))]` + `[PartCreationPolicy(CreationPolicy.Shared)]` on CourseService do together?

options.text: Publish the class as the ICourseService implementation, as a single shared instance
Create a new ICourseService for every import
Mark CourseService as a POCO entity

items.explanation: [Export] publishes the part as the named interface; CreationPolicy.Shared makes MEF hand out one shared instance.

misconceptions.b: Shared means a single instance; NonShared would create one per import.

items.stem: In one or two sentences: how does a sink end up holding its destination service, given Synnduit uses MEF (not Microsoft.Extensions.DI)?
rubric: The service class is published with [Export(typeof(IService))] (often [PartCreationPolicy(Shared)])
The sink's constructor is marked [ImportingConstructor]; MEF matches the export to the constructor parameter and injects it
items.sampleAnswer: The service is exported with [Export(typeof(IService))] as a shared part. The sink's [ImportingConstructor] tells MEF which constructor to build; MEF finds the matching export and passes it into that constructor.

items.stem: You have `class CourseService : ICourseService` and a `CourseSink`. Add the MEF attributes that publish CourseService as a single shared part and the attribute that lets MEF inject it into CourseSink's constructor.
rubric: [ImportingConstructor] on the CourseSink constructor that takes ICourseService
